items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: These are serious issues
and they deserve better than the drivel we ha ve just listened to from Andrew Williams.
10 Apr 2013 Urgent Debates 9225
These are important issues, and, as Alan Ma rtin would say, it is the putting right that
counts. The great thing about wh at has happened here is that a secretive spy agency has
been exposed to sunlight, has been exposed to  a cold, hard review, and that is what I
want to focus on this after noon. I certainly do not want to  focus on the unprofessional
comments of Sir Bruce Ferguson, who was seen  deep in conversation with Geoffrey
Palmer on Lambton Quay this afternoon. I ce rtainly do not intend this afternoon to
comment on the role of “H3”, as he then was, when he served Helen Clark and Heather
Simpson on level nine. What did Mr Robert son know, and when did he know it? He is
the one who had quite a number of interac tions with the Government Communications
Security Bureau when he was “H3”, and it is going to be very interesting to explore that
issue in the months to come.
What I want to focus on—and focusing on principles, not personalities—are two
issues. The first is the 2003 legislation, the Government  Communications Security
Bureau Act. Mr Goff was one of those nodding automatons in the Cabinet committee
who approved the bill for introduction. The fact of the matter is that this legislation was
drafted when Helen Clark was Prime Minister. It went through Parliament very quickly.
It was a classic case of legislative neglig ence, quite frankly. It  was drafted by the
Government Communications Security Bureau. It was not tested independently.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Who voted for it?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: The Government Communications Security
Bureau assumptions and advice were relied on, and it was a totally unsatisfactory way
of making law, for which I say to Mr Robertso n that all parties in this House bear some
responsibility, although I do observe—I do observe—that th e Labour Party at that time
was riding triumphant. It had 52 seats, al though over the detested foreshore and seabed
legislation it was shortly to lose a few me mbers. We had 27, but we stand up and say
that in so far as we voted for it, there are questions that, looking forward, we do need to

Russel Norman relied on, is clear enough on its terms, but then you go to the definition
of what is a “foreign person” or a “for eign organisation”, and there are difficult

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Very clear-cut.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: They are matters that were identified—well,
I suggest, and I am quite happy to talk off-lin e to Mr Robertson a bout the definition of
“foreign organisation”, because it is not clear. Go to the passage and look at it, and the
member will find that his superficial, third-rate analysis is inadequate.
The other thing that needs to be addresse d is that the legislation needs to be
redrafted, but we also need to look at issues of complia nce—issues that go back for
years. Frankly, when I read the Kitteridge report, I was not at all happy, because the Act
is one thing, but there was no reference in  the legal section of the Government
Communications Security Bureau to any othe r legislation. There was no reference to
clear international law texts. There was no re ference to jurisprudence—for example, the
Supreme Court judgment recently on the issue of spying in the Ureweras, the Hamed
case, was not referred to. And it is important —and I say this in answer to some of the
questions that were be ing raised this afternoon by the Green Pa rty co-leader about the
Crown Law Office involvement, because he is  right: the Crown Law Office is there to
provide authoritative legal ad vice for the Crown, and it is very important for every
public sector organisation to keep close to that organisation. But, as the report says on
page 25, it did not. Twelve opinions were provided by Crown Law to the Government
Communications Security Bureau between 1988 and September 2012—24 years—and
only three dealt with operational matters, but in the last 6 months 10 opinions have been
provided.
9226 Urgent Debates 10 Apr 2013
So, quite frankly, there is a lot to be learnt from this exercise, but the legal
compliance, the fundamental primer 1 comp liance that Sir Bruce Ferguson and others
should have been looking at over the years, did not happe n, and it is totally
unsatisfactory. For all the cries and the screams, and, as I said, the adolescent piffle that
we heard from Andrew Williams, let us get down to what the issues are and what the
issues are not. It is important to get this right going forward. It is very good that this
secretive organisation has been exposed to s unlight, and, as I said, it is the putting right
that counts.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Talking of negligence, one wonders
what role the Attorney-General did not play in advice to the Prime Minister. He is full
of sound and fury now, but was obviously pretty  silent when it came to giving advice to

Some members of this House will be  well aware of that comic strip Spy vs. Spy . It
was first seen in the Mad magazine in about 1961. I am pleased to say it is still going. It
is great political satire, and many of us have had a good laugh over the years. Well, I
have to say that in New Zeal and over the past 2 weeks we have seen behaviour straight
out of the Mad magazine. If it was not so serious , you could have believed that the
whole thing was a political spoof or political satire.
I mean, we have just heard from the Atto rney-General about conspiracy theories—
someone was seen talking to someone up Lambton Quay. Well, I believe that most of us
who walk up Lambton Quay meet somebody we know—maybe people we do not even
like—and we might even talk to them. But heavens, this is now a conspiracy! But I have
to say I thought the whole thing was summed  up this week in a cartoon by Emmerson.

items.speaker: Here it is. It says
items.text: “Spy vs. Lie”. Here we have the Government Communications
Security Bureau as the black  spy, and here we have John Key as the white spy saying:
“Psst! I think they’re on to us.” Well, I think that sums it up.
John Key has to get the award for the best shimmy in living memory, because he has
been caught out. He has been caught out on his terminological inexactitudes over
Dotcom. He got caught out on his less than honest answers about the appointment of the
Director of the Government Communications Security Burea u. He said on Tuesday: “I

following week he said: “Well, you know, I did know him a bit better. He knew my
brother.” It has been a movi ng feast as to whether he kne w him or whether he did not
know him. The truth is that he knew hi m well enough to have his number in his
telephone book. I have to say I do not think I have got any of my primary school
friends’ numbers in my phone. I did have a qui ck look to see whether I had any. I have
not got them, but he does. He does not know him very well, he hardly remembers him,
but there is the telephone number.
He also got exposed over the dates and the times that he knew about illegal spying on
88 New Zealanders. He got confused over what he knew and where and how. It is really

issue. Now he has performed a beautiful political shimmy. He has shifted the blame
from himself and his inadequacy on to inadequate  legislation. This is legislation that we
heard from the Attorney-General is inadequa te, that is very badly drafted, that the
National Party voted for, that it looked at at the select co mmittee and supported, and
that has been in place since 2003.
I have to say that if you us e the Prime Minister’s standard of behaviour, he must step
down from his position as the head of the Government Communications Security
Bureau. He ought to stand down right away if  he is to follow through with his own
standard. After all, think of the standard he applied to Nick Smith, to Pansy Wong, to
10 Apr 2013 Urgent Debates 9227
Richard Worth, to Phil Heatley, and to Ka te Wilkinson. He would be gone before
breakfast if he applied that standard to his behaviour in terms of this whole issue.
He is the only Prime Minister in the last decade who has been told that his agency
was spying illegally—the only Prime Minister who has been told this, and that is a fact.
He was told in July last year. He covered it up for 9 long months. It only came out in the
Kitteridge report. Did he do something about it,  as we have asked today? Did he move
to stop it spying illegally? No, he did not. He hoped it wo uld not come out, and he
covered it up for 9 months. He had no plan in place as to what he was going to do. He
put the issue on the back-burner because he wanted to have all those photo opportunities
over in China, but he got caught out. He got  caught out, and New Zealanders, I believe,
cannot have confidence in a leader with his record. They  cannot have confidence in a
leader who cannot remember, who cannot perform, and who covers up.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: It is worth reflecting on what the key
issues are associated with this debate and with this issue. There is a role for the
Government Communications Security Bureau  in New Zealand—that is agreed by
virtually all parties in th is Parliament—and the previous Government brought in
legislation in the early 2000s to legitimise th is. In the legislation they made it very
express that the bureau was not to spy on New Zealanders. That is what they did in that
legislation. But there was another piece of legislation that also said that the bureau could
work with other agencies as appropriate. So this comes down to a fine legal point of two
potentially conflicting features of legislat ion: working with ot her agencies, or not
surveilling New Zealanders. That was the issu e. What has come out of this case and out
of the Kitteridge report are those issues—that fine contrast between those two cases.
Clearly what has happened here is the Government Communications Security Bureau
has been working with other agencies, at thei r request, believing, as it did, that the law
provided it with the scope to do  that. So it then assisted t hose other agencies with their
work on people whom those other agencies ha d legitimate authority of one sort or
another to monitor or surveil or do whatever they were doing with them. Those agencies
that had those people in their sights had a legi timate and legal right to surveil, monitor,
or do whatever they were doing with those pe ople. They then asked the bureau, because
of its unique equipment and skills, to support them in that work. The bureau believed,
because of its interpretation of the law, that  it was entitled to s upport those agencies. It
is not a question of the bureau illegally survei lling a number of New Zealanders. It is a
question of the fact that they  thought that, in support of th e other agencies that were
legally monitoring or surveilli ng these individuals, they were doing what they were
doing in a lawful way.
What has clearly come out of the Kitteridge  report is the fact that there is this
confusion over the legislation, and that need s to be dealt with—a nd the Prime Minister
has said as much. But those cases now, th e so-called 88, are being referred to the
Inspector-General of Intelligence and Securit y, who is the legal authority to determine
whether or not there has been a breach of the legislation. That is set out in the law. It is
up to the inspector-general to decide whether or not there has been illegality. What we
know from the Kitteridge  report is that ther e are questions over that  legality resulting
from the lack of clarity now about the two legal provisions. That is what it is about here.
It is quite wrong for Opposition members to make the comments that they do. How
do we know that the Prime Minister is the onl y Prime Minister whom these issues were
ever raised with? How do we know? How do we know whether this was the case? How
do we know whether Sir Bruce Ferguson never raised it with Helen Clark? How do we
know whether this happened or not? What we  do know is that this hinges on a very
technical interpretation of two clauses in the law. That is what the Kitteridge report
says, and that is why the inspector-general will investigate those. That is what is set out
9228 Urgent Debates 10 Apr 2013
in the law. It is clear that in the case of  the 88 people who were being surveilled or
monitored, it was being done with the proper le gal authority of the agencies that were
doing that. The law does allow the SIS to spy on New Zealanders—OK. So those
people were allowed to be spied on. The conf usion relates to the legal provisions that
allowed the Government Communications Secur ity Bureau to assist the SIS and other
agencies. That happened under Labour, and it  happened under Nation al. It will fall to
National to work with other parties in this Parliament to fix those provisions. It is a very
fine technical point, established in the Kitteridge report.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It gives me pleasure to follow my
colleague Tony Ryall, who I thi nk has laid out very clearly the real issues that we are
facing here today. Firstly, it is important that we understand that the New Zealand SIS is
able to spy on New Zealanders if there is a warrant, which means there is a court
process, and if, in order to get that, it has very good reasons to suspect that people are
up to nefarious activities. So the New Zealand SIS is entitled to spy on New Zealanders.
Under the Government Communications Security  Bureau Act, which has been in place
now for 10 years—and we have heard my collea gues in this House explain that, yes, it
was passed under Labour in 2003—there was a provision put in th at said the bureau
could not spy on New Zealanders. But th e practice was continued. The bureau and
organisations like the New Zealand SIS, the New Zealand Police, and the New Zealand
Defence Force believed the pr actice was legal because of so me legal technicalities, and
that the bureau could use the very expert technology, skills, and resources that it has to
act as agents for those other organisations . Those other organisations would have the
legal right to spy on or surveil or monitor individuals in New Zeal and or organisations
in New Zealand that they had evidence that a court had agreed was sufficient to enable
that monitoring. So this was an attempt to ac t on behalf of, and to use the surveillance
mechanisms that they have in place. And everyone believed they were acting within the
law—everyone. That has happened for the last 10 years, under both the previous Labour
Government and under this New Zealand National Government.
The second issue that I think needs to be put in  play here, as we  look at what the
issues are and how we resolve them, is that we are in a very different world
technologically today and, as a result of the increasing developments in technology, we
face from a cyber-security perspective much different threats than we faced even 10
years ago, when the Government Communica tions Security Bureau Act was passed
through this House. So we have agencies that are dealing with  a whole range of
different organisations and methods of co mmitting cyber-crime that perhaps were not
envisaged 10 years ago. I think those are th e two issues: first of all, that we have
legislation that does allow interception, monitoring, of New Zealanders, and that people
believed that they were acting in good faith and within the bounds of the law.
I think we in New Zealand are very lucky that we have a Prime Minister like John
Key, who, when it was brought to his attention that there was some doubt as to whether
these practices were legal and the risks that we ran if they were not legal, took
immediate action. He put in Rebecca Kitterid ge to do an enormous review of the
Government Communications Security Bureau , in order to make sure that that
organisation was well positioned, both legally and capacity wise, to deal with the real
threats that the modern world poses to New Zealand. I think th e Kitteridge review,
which is a very hard-hitting, pull-no-punches re view, is excellent. I have no doubt that
this House, given the comments that have been made today, wants to address the issues,
and I look forward to the suppor t in this House for putting ri ght the legislation that will
enable those organisations that have the re sponsibility for ensuring the security of New
Zealand to get on and do their jobs and be confident that they are acting within the law.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: There are two problems with the
Kitteridge report. The first is that the Kitt eridge report does not examine the critical
issue, which was the role of John Key in exercising his ministerial responsibility to have
oversight of the Government Communications Security Bureau. It cannot do that. It was
unfair to expect Rebecca Kitteridge to do that . She is Secretary of the Cabinet. She is
having day-to-day meetings with the Prime Minister. Is that why the Prime Minister
chose a person who could not go to the hear t of this problem and say: “Why was the
Minister responsible for the GCSB unable to  do his job of exercising adequate and
proper oversight of this agency?”
You know, we give our spy agencies incred ible power. We need them—people have
talked about cyber-attacks, and that is quite  right—but they have incredible power, and
they exercise that power with total se crecy. We therefore rely on the Minister
responsible for the GCSB to make sure that safeguards, checks, and balances are in
place to ensure that that agency behaves legitimately, under the law, and in a proper
way. I have to say this: John Key failed absolutely in that responsibility.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I remember John Key as Prime Minister in 2009, Anne Tolley,
coming into this House and saying that he  would expect higher  standards of his
Ministers. Those higher standa rds, surely, need to involve competence, they need to
involve a readiness to exercise proper oversi ght, and they need to involve a readiness to
be open and transparent. On every one of t hose criteria John Key failed. By his own
standards, he should have sacked himself as Minister responsible for the GCSB. He
failed on every one of those fronts.
But there is a second thing that the Kitteridge report fails to do. The Kitteridge report
fails to go to the heart of where this affa ir began, which was the raid on Kim Dotcom’s
house. The first thing we know about that is th at we went in with a combination of the
Keystone Cops and Rambo—I do not know  which is more appropriate as a
description—with helicopters and the Special Tactics Group—

items.speaker: Hon Chester Borrows
items.text: You Labour guys love the police, eh?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: —full use of force, and for what, Mr Borrows? And for what? To
issue an extradition warrant for copyright infringement!
Can anybody in the world belie ve that the New Zealand Mi nister of Police allowed
her police to go in, fully armed, with helicopters, as if it wa s an attack on Hanoi during
the Viet Nam War, all to serve an extr adition warrant and to seize a couple of
computers? It was bizarre. You know, pr obably the police and the Government
Communications Security Bureau wanted to  impress their colleagues in the United
States, the FBI. Far from impressing them, sadly, they showed their utter incompetence
in the way they carried out that role, and I hold the Government Ministers responsible
for their failure of oversight.
Secondly, they went in, in this dramatic wa y, without the legal authority to do so. A
High Court judge in this country, Justice Helen Winkelmann, found that they had no
right of search or seizure and they had an invalid warrant. So when Chris Finlayson as
the Attorney-General gets up to spout in th is House, I want to know why there was so
much incompetence and how you could conduct a raid that will make New Zealand
liable for tens of millions of dollars in legal suits from Kim Dotcom. I want to know
why there was so much incompetence, and why there is not an inquiry into that facet.
Then there is the third aspect of that raid , and that is that Kim Dotcom and a number
of other people were subjected to a month of covert surveillance without there being the
legal right to conduct that surveillance. That  is correct, Mr Brownlee, is it not? There
was no legal right to conduct that  surveillance. They said they did it on the basis, Mr
Brownlee, that they did not know that he was a New Zealand resident. But the
9230 Urgent Debates 10 Apr 2013
Immigration Service had told them that ve ry shortly afterwards, and your Government
concealed it from the public—it told them that they had acted illegally, but your
Government concealed it from the public.
But John Key concealed something much wo rse than that. For the first time a
Minister in charge of the New Zealand Securi ty Intelligence Service was told that there
had been spying for a significant period of time in a comprehensive way and that the
legal authority to do that was in doubt. John Key was told that in July.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: 19th of March.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: How do I know he was told that in July? Because he said so
yesterday in his press statement. He was told that in July. Then for 9 long months he sat
on that. He did not just sit on it—when he was asked in Se ptember whether this was an
isolated incident, he said yes, it was an isolated incident. John Key knew he was not
telling the truth. He knew that he was not telling the truth. He had known since July that
there had been a pattern of activity that wa s illegal. And did he tell the New Zealand
public? Not a word for 9 months. For 9 months he kept that from the public.
John Key has a parliamentary committee, th e Intelligence and Security Committee,
which should have the right to  know that sort of informa tion. During that 9 months did
he call the committee together, to give the parliamentary oversight that that committee
was set up to provide, and tell it the truth? No, he did not. So John Key needs to come
into this House and say why he would not front up to the New Zealand public and why
he would not front up to th e parliamentary Intelligence and Security Committee and tell
them the truth about what the agency that he as a Minister is responsible for was
actually doing.
But there is more to it than that. Can we  really believe that John Key did not know
anything about what was happening in th e biggest operation that New Zealand has
mounted in association with  the United States on New Z ealand soil, involving the
Ministry of Justice, involving the Crown Law Office, involving the Police, involving
the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and involving the Government
Communications Security Bureau? Can we really believe that as being credible?
Can we then believe that the Governme nt Communications Security Bureau for
months and months and months never told him the truth about th e illegality of the
actions? Well, you know, there are a couple of explanations. One is dishonesty and
incompetence and an arrogant disregard for the rights of New Zealanders to know. Sir
Bruce Ferguson came up with another explanat ion, and he said it publicly. That is very
unusual for a top civil servant. He loyally se rved the country for four decades. He said:
“When I dealt with John Key, he wasn’t inte rested in what we were doing.” But that
does not explain why he was never told by Ian Fletcher, because Ian Fletcher was the
man whom he had personally hand-picked, in  breach of the normal procedures of the
State Services Commission, to put in—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: It’s not true.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: It is true, and Iain Rennie made it clear that it was highly unusual
for him to do that. That is Yes, Minister talk for: “I was astonished and I was shocked
that he did it.” He went in  and he hand-picked his own person to head the Government
Communications Security Bureau. He did not just hand-pick the person. There was only
one interview—one interview—and they c hose the person who interviewed best. One
interview—that really smells.
The Prime Minister is meant to be the Minist er in charge of that agency. He is meant
to know what is going on, and he is meant to hold it accountable, and he failed on every
front. But can we believe this, too? Bill English signed a ministerial warrant covering
up the role of the Gove rnment Communications Security Bureau in this affair. That has
never been done in New Zealand’s history before—
10 Apr 2013 Urgent Debates 9231

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Tell us about Bruce Ferguson.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: —Chris Finlayson. It has ne ver been done. Can you really
believe that Bill English took an unprecedented step, acting as Prime Minister, and
never told John Key when he came back to New Zealand that he had signed this warrant
covering the matter up? It has never been done  in history, and he did not bother to tell
John Key? Hey, pull the other arm. Nobody believes that.
The fact is that this affair smells. It smells in every aspect. There have been too many
brain fades. There have been too many lies by omission. There have been too many
times when the Government has not been prep ared to be open and transparent. As Chris
Finlayson quoted before, Oliver Wendell Ho lmes said that “Sunlight is the best
disinfectant.”, and what we need is a full and independent inquiry to allow the sun to
shine in on this murky affair.
This is a serious issue, but that was a ve ry sad speech from Phil Goff. It was a sad
speech on a number of points. Firstly, a great deal of it was simply fanciful, made up by
Phil Goff to suit the mantra of the Labour Party. He is a man who was formerly the
chairman of the Cabinet external relations and defence committee, and who also sat on
the Intelligence and Security Committee and th erefore, for a very long time, presided
over the illegal activit ies that have affected 88 New Zealanders since 2003. He comes
into this House and starts pointing the finge r at the current Prime Minister, who has had
the courage to say: “No more. We’re sending in  someone to make an inquiry so we find
out exactly where the weaknesses are, so we can sort it out.”
The Labour Party knows that this is a minor i ssue. It knows that it is a fine point of
law that we are dealing with, and if Labour was really serious, then today it would not
have had Grant Robertson request the spec ial debate; it would have had its leader,
David Shearer, request the special debate. Why did Labour not ge t David Shearer to
lead the debate today? Well, the problem is that the first speech is a 15-minute speech,
and Labour could not guarantee that by the tim e David Shearer got to  the end of it he
would remember what the debate was about. Phil Goff over there talks about
forgetfulness and about omissions and all th e rest of it. Well, the biggest forgetful
moment in this House—the greatest omission in  this House—demonstrated this year is
the secret bank account of David Shearer, whic h he still will not tell New Zealanders
about.
What you have got is essentia lly a party trying to create  a degree of outrage over
what is a very fine point of confusion be tween the two spy agencies in New Zealand.
The Security Intelligence Service can, with  a warrant, spy on New Zealanders. It can
intercept. It can surveil. What it has done for years, for decades, is, in fact, get hold of
the Government Communications Security Bureau to do that listening capability. That
is where the problem has come from, because the Government Communications
Security Bureau does not have the legal right to do that. That is what this report from
Rebecca Kitteridge makes very clear, and the Government response is that that will be
cleared up.
I want to turn also to a couple of points that  Miss Kitteridge has put in her report that

items.speaker: I think are particularly important. She says
items.text: “The time I have spent within GCSB has
left me in no doubt that New Zealand needs this organisation now more than ever. The
increasing threat of cyber attacks and the protec tive role GCSB plays is one part of this
story, but GCSB does a wide rang e of other things that are essential to the well-being
and prosperity of New Zealand.” That is a very powerful statement from someone who
went into the organisation wanting to know where the bad bits were and what the good
bits were. When the report is boiled right down, we get to that very fine legal point that
can be fixed up.
9232 Urgent Debates 10 Apr 2013
What we have heard from the Labour Party is it is throwing  in all sorts of other red
herrings, particularly around the appointment of the new chief executive—the chief spy,
if you like—of New Zealand, Mr Ian Fletcher. Can I say for a start that I was fascinated
by the speech from Russel Norman, where he decided—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Ha!

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Well, it does not happen very  often, but it did on this
occasion. He decided to quote from David Lange’s book, where he said in that book
effectively that when he was Prime Mini ster he had no idea what the Government
Communications Security Bureau was up to, that it would not tell him anything, and
that it just went about its busin ess as if he did not exist. Well, the odd thing is that he
got to appoint the chief spy. So I want to  know why he appointed someone who would
not tell him what was going on. What that show s, I think, is a general omission that you
get from the left of politics in New Zeala nd, which wants to say that the rights of
criminals are just as great as the rights of those who are o ffended against. I, for one, do
not accept that.
When it comes right down to it, the appointment is made by the Prime Minister. I
cannot for 1 minute believe that Helen Clark did not make a personal approach to Sir
Bruce Ferguson. I believe that Mr Key has, in identifying Mr Flet cher, recognised that
he needs someone from way outside the system , not someone who is sort of in the club
and part of the network, but someone who is very, very far and remote from it, who has
an excellent Public Service record in other jurisdictions, and who can come in and clean
up the outfit. But we cannot lose sight of the fact that this is an essential organisation for
New Zealand and that it must continue to exist.
I think the other things that have been  mentioned this afternoon have all been
designed to perhaps get the media excited about lit tle bits of this and little bits of that,
losing sight of the big challe nge that this organisation has. I turn again to Miss
Kitteridge’s report at point 183, which says: “My belief in the importance of the work
carried out by the men and women at GCSB has only increased as this review has
proceeded. The world is becoming more complex, and physical borders are less
relevant. The nature of the thre ats to national security is shifting so rapidly that keeping
up with them is a challenge—let alone getting ahead.”
So let us be clear. We have the Security  Intelligence Service surveilling some New
Zealanders because, presumably, they were id entified as being ratbags and up to things
that were not good for this country, were not good for our economy, were not good for
wider prosperity, and were unreasonable for New Zealanders to have to put up with. To
help it in that work, the Security Inte lligence Service effectively contracted the
Government Communications Security Bure au to do the listening side of that
surveillance. That was not legal. That is well accepted. That is noted. The Prime
Minister knew formally of that on 19 March this year and I think has acted
appropriately ever since. The outrage that you get from the other side of the House is
somewhat laughable.
Can I just point to the comments that cam e from the New Zealand First Party. There
has never been a party in this Parliament that has been softer on crime than New
Zealand First—utterly pathetic, always on the side of the criminal, always wanting to
put forward the rights of the so-called oppressed in the justice system. The member who
spoke, Andrew Williams, talked about the lack of memory that seems, in his opinion, to
have characterised this whole saga. Well, I have simply got to say one thing to him. Go
back to the office, Mr Williams. Go into Mr Peters’ office and say: “What was it that
made you forget a $100,000 donation to the New Zealand First Party and then go out
publicly and say that you forgot about it?”. Th is is a serious issue of the pot calling the
kettle black.
10 Apr 2013 Urgent Debates 9233
No one’s history in this particular issue is good. Since 2003, when the Government
Communications Security Bureau was finally put into a legislative framework, there has
been a series of illegal surv eillances carried out. No one denies that, but it is quite
reasonable that there could have been a mi stake or a misunderstanding between the two
sides, the two agencies of State in this particular case.
In conclusion, my point is simply this . The Labour Party has had an enormous
amount of fun over the last few weeks, trying to  ramp this up into something that it is
not. It is one of those things that has unf ortunately happened, but it has been exposed
and made certain only by the fact that Rebecca Kitteridge was sent by the Prime
Minister into the Government  Communications Security Bur eau to investigate what the
situation was. There is a commitment from the Government and a commitment from the
Prime Minister that he will talk to other parties. We know that the Labour Party will not
support the legislation, New Zealand First will not support the legislation, and the
Greens do not want anybody who does anything ille gal to be confronted at all, so they
will not support the legislation, but the sens ible parties in this  House will pass the
legislation in order to make it clear that th is sort of activity cannot continue in the
future. I think this is all summed up by the fact that the leader of the Labour Party was
himself not prepared to lead this debate this afternoon.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I move, That the House take note of
miscellaneous business . That has been a very interesting debate on the Government
Communications Security Bureau and what it shows us is that Ne w Zealanders cannot
trust this John Key - led National Governme nt. We have seen confidence in this
Government reach basement level over the last  2 or 3 weeks. In fact, there has been a
slow drip, drip, drip on the stone of conf idence now for about the last year. It has
reached basement bottom now, and why? Because what we have from the National
Government is a lot of very  arrogant members, who are very dismissive of any
suggestions, ideas, or debates that do not suit their ideas. They are ve ry evasive in their
answers. In fact, in this House I have seen the worst answering of parliamentary
questions I have seen in decades and we have  also seen diversions. Whenever an issue
arises that they are not happy with, they set up a diversion. They usually use Paula
Bennett to pull out yet one more of her welfar e reforms so that they can head off over
there bashing up beneficiaries, because that always gets a good headline. So what we
have got is a Government that cannot be trusted. It would rather not front up to the
issues; it would rather divert from them.
I think the biggest diversion is the Prime Minister, who heads off to China to get
plenty of publicity, knowing that at home there was a report into the Government
Communications Security Bureau that show ed he did nothing fo r 9 months—that he
allowed illegal spying to continue on New Zealanders for 9 months. I think it was
summed up by the Dominion Post with this headline that said “Illegal spying kept secret
for months”—illegal spying kept  secret for months. So he heads off to China and he
leaves his hapless team here in New Zeala nd. Only somebody leaked the report. Well, I
have got a theory about this: Mr Key wanted th e report to be leaked. He wanted it to be
leaked, because poor old Bill English is havi ng to stand up in this House day after day
facing a barrage of questions, difficult questions, that John Key does not want to face.
He is hoping that when he gets back from  China this might have all blown over and
there will be another diversion created by th e National Government. Well, I can tell Mr
Key that this is far too seri ous for him to think that this  is going to go away, because
9234 General Debate 10 Apr 2013
what we need to have is an independent inquiry and review of the Government
Communications Security Bureau and, in my vi ew, the SIS and the roles that they play
in New Zealand. We need that independent re view, not some idea that has come from
John Key.
What did he say on the televi sion this morning? He said he is going to change the
law. He said he is going to bring in legislation to allow the Government
Communications Security Bureau to legally  spy on New Zealanders. Well, to begin
with, he is going to do that with no consulta tion with anyone in this House. He has not
taken it to the very committee that has been se t up for him to consult with. He just gets
on television and says he is going to change the law and make illegal spying legal. That
is not the way you deal with an issue like this. You do not  go for the quick-fix, fast-
draw solution. You work through the issues  carefully. Perhaps you might even use the
legal brain of Chris Finlayson in this respect, but you do not suddenly announce on
television that you are going to  change the law and the rest of us are all meant to trot
along behind. That is not how it is going to be done, and we are going to demand in this
Parliament across the Opposition that there is a proper review of the Government
Communications Security Bureau and the SI S—a proper look at the roles they play. I
would be very concerned if we were to put together both those ro les, because the only
countries that I know of that do that are thos e that have authoritarian Governments, that
have organisations like the KGB. We have separated out those two roles and we need to
look very carefully before we make such changes.
New Zealanders have every right to lose  confidence in this Government. Illegal
spying—what a mess! Then we have all the privacy breaches—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Under your watch.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Nick Smith says it was on our watch. Let us deal with that.
He is such a brain that he sat in the Oppos ition, looked at the legislation that Labour
brought in, it went through a select committee,  and did he vote for it? Yes, Nick Smith,
the brains trust of the National Party, voted for it. It was all right then; suddenly it is not.
New Zealanders have every right to be very suspicious of this Government.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: How ironic that we
have Annette King, a member of the previ ous Labour Government’s Cabinet, who has

items.text: No troubles then.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: “No troubles then.”, she says —“No troubles then at all.”

We get this sort of faux, mock anger o ccasionally. I notice that Mr Twyford there

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: I would like to speak about the security and
intelligence travesty called the Government Communications Security Bureau.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Name and party.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: The failure of Governments to get control and deep
oversight of this foreign-dominated in telligence beast and its unsavoury Echelon
alliance—and apparently I should state that I am speaking for the Green Party on this.
New Zealand as an independent State should have a role in prom oting civil rights and
peace, reducing conflict, confronting injustice, and protecting the environment. We have
shown an example with our nuclear-free po licy. However, operating the eavesdropping
facilities of the Government Communications Security Bureau’s bases at Waihopai and
Tangimoana makes a mockery of New Zealan ders’ preferred peace-based role in the
world.
First announced in 1987, Waihopai is opera ted by the Government Communications
Security Bureau in the inte rests of the foreign powers gr ouped together in the very
super-secret UK-USA agreement known as Eche lon. Echelon shares global electronic
and signals intelligence among the spy agenci es of the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and
New Zealand. Waihopai’s satelli te interception dishes in tercept a huge volume of
civilian telephone calls, telexes, faxes, em ail, and computer data communications.
Waihopai spies variously on Latin America,  Russia, China, Japan, other Asian
neighbours of ours, our very cl ose friends in the South Paci fic, and now, illegally, also
on us—New Zealanders. This material is fo rwarded on to the major partners in the UK-
USA agreement, specifically the US National Security Agency, the NSA. Mr English in
his faux pas today, speaking on behalf of the Government Communications Security
Bureau, would have been a lot more accurate if he had said he was speaking on behalf
of the USA.
Waihopai’s targets are international civilian communications, including the
interception of New Zealanders’ internationa l phone calls. New Zealanders will also be
really intrigued to know that their mobiles, even when they are not speaking on them as
10 Apr 2013 General Debate 9237
such, are effectively Government Communications Security Bureau microphones, if that
is the will of the spy agencies—or maybe of the Prime Minister.
Nicky Hager’s book published back in 1996, Secret Power: New Zealand’s Role in
the International Spy Network, included a foreword by David Lange: “In the mid-1980s
we bucked the system. We may have been ah ead of our time on matters nuclear, but we
were out of step with what was called the ‘Western Alliance’. It took a break with the
United States and Britain to make the people of New Zealand aware that we were part
of an international intelligence organisati on which had its roots in a different world
order and which could command compliance fr om us while withholding from us the
benefits of others’ in telligence.” He went on: “Life at  the time was full of unpleasant
surprises. State-sponsored te rrorism was a crime against humanity as long as it wasn’t
being practiced by the allies, when it was studi ously ignored. In the national interest it
became necessary to say ‘ouch’ and frown and bear certain reprisals of our intelligence
partners. We even went the length of buildi ng a satellite station at Waihopai.”—in my
words, for the USA and maybe the UK. Lange  continued that “it was not until I read
this book that I had any idea that we had b een committed to an international integrated
electronic network.” So even the Prime Mini ster of the day did not know what our
security chiefs had hooked us into.
But now we have got John Key wanting to le gitimise his mate Ian Fletcher’s illegal
spying on New Zealanders for the USA, and it was not just Ian Fletcher; it obviously
went on for some time before that. But it suited to carry on for the 88 people that little
bit longer until they realised they could not get away with it any longer. Waihopai needs
closing down. The Government Communications Security Bureau has been given well
over $600 million of taxpayers’ money in the past two decades.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: This afternoon I want to talk
about a subject that will affect all of us at some point in our lives. A few days ago I saw
a billboard that said that 15 pe rcent of the children born this y ear will live to be well in
excess of 100 years. The issue that that high lighted, and highlights for us, is the issue of
superannuation. This country has been grappli ng with that issue unsatisfactorily, really,
for the last 30 years.
At the last election we saw the position taken by the two major parties, which was a
polarised extreme in many senses: the National Party saying that the age of entitlement
will remain 65 in perpetuity, e ffectively; the Labour Party sa ying that over a period of
time it wishes to raise the age to 67. The problem with both those positions is as
follows: one is inflexible, and the other impos es a burden on working people to stay in
the workforce well beyond the time that they might have planned to retire.
We are starting to see a rising tide of public information and public questioning now
about the viability of the system. No one is  seriously suggesting that we should cut the
pension—no one apart from th e far right. No one is seri ously suggesting a radical
9238 General Debate 10 Apr 2013
increase in the age of entitlement. But what  people are seeking is more flexibility and
more choice, and I note with interest a recent newspaper survey that put a couple of
propositions before New Zealanders. When people were asked whether they favoured
the status quo of 65, raising the qualifying age to 67, or giving people the option of
retiring later for a bit more or earlier fo r a bit less, nearly 50 percent—49 percent—
favoured the flexible approach. The status  quo was favoured by 29 percent, and 15
percent wanted to go to 67.
Within that survey is the answer to the question that New Zealand confronts, and that
is why United Future, as part of its conf idence and supply agreement, is promoting the
concept of flexible superannuation. A person w ho makes the choice to retire early at,
say, 60 would get around 65 percent of th e core entitlement of New Zealand
superannuation, the person reti ring at 65 would get 100 perc ent, and the person who
chose to defer retirement unt il age 70, or to defer pi cking up their superannuation,
would get around 130 percent of th e core entitlement. What th at recognises is a couple
of things: firstly, New Zealanders are working longer and, secondly—and probably
most important in the context of this de bate—they want the choice about when they
retire. They do not want to be told by the Stat e that they have got to work 2 more years,
to 67, to qualify. They are uncertain about the viability of 65. They want to be able to
arrange their affairs in a way that they can make the choice.
What makes this policy even more attractiv e is that with the increasing uptake of
KiwiSaver, in years to come we will have many, many more New Zealanders qualifying
for a KiwiSaver payout at the age of 65. So the argument that is raised by some, that
you cannot afford to retire early on a reduced rate of superannuation, will be diminished
by the fact that people actually know that there is a big nest egg coming at 65.
Flexible superannuation provides an answer to the issue that confronts New Zealand.
It does not cut the overa ll level of pension expenditure, bu t it certainly stabilises it. It
gives New Zealanders more c hoice about when they retire, and people who feel that
they are physically exhausted long before 65 can make some plans with certainty about
picking up superannuation at a re duced rate at an earlier time. Others who feel hale and
hearty, or who are in a position where they  are financially independent, could well
choose to work later and then pick up their superannuation later.
There will be, within the next few months, a discussion paper issued publicly, as part
of our confidence and supply agreement, i nviting public feedback on this issue. But
what I note with interest is the overwhel ming support that the newspaper poll indicated
already, before this issue ha s really had a huge amount of traction in the public. I note
also the interest that I have had from the Leader  of the Opposition and from
Government Ministers.
This is an idea whose time is rapidly co ming. New Zealanders know that things have
got to change. If you go back 50 years, the age profile in New Zealand was the classic
Christmas tree. Now it looks much more like a lamppost. It is probably going to become
more like an inverted Christmas tree in the future. What we have to do now is plan for
that time and put in place a sensible appro ach to superannuation th at is sustainable and
that will last for future generations, and Flexi Super is that answer.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Today 1,300 food service workers who work in our
public hospitals were told by the Minister of  Health, Tony Ryall, and this Government
that they are just back-office workers—just  back-office workers. These are the 1,300
workers up and down the country in every ho spital, in small towns and large, who
prepare, cook, and serve meals to hospita l patients—those people who are in hospital
relying on decent, nutritious, and healthy food in  their recovery after illness or surgery.
That comment from the Minister Tony Ry all shows just how much regard this
Government has for hard-working New Zeala nders who are out th ere doing their best,
10 Apr 2013 General Debate 9239
trying to do their best for the community and their families, and that is why we cannot
trust the John Key - led Government. Those people, from what Tony Ryall said today,
are just figures on paper. They are not real people; they are dollars  to be mined on an
already stretched budget. There are no worri es, no concerns, about  the families and
communities that will be affected, no concer ns about what will happen to those hard-
working New Zealanders and their families, and no worries that there are another 1,300
jobs on the line, to add to the thousands and thousa nds that are part of this
Government’s disgraceful record of job loss and failure to do anything about it.
Today the Minister and the Government not only demonstrated their ignorance about
the work that our food service workers do in our public hospitals but also demonstrated
their complete ignorance about  the difference between cont racting in and contracting
out. Let us be clear. This is not about f ood service workers in hospitals working for
contractors, as, indeed, many already do; this is about cl osing hospital kitchens and
having food shipped in from central food pr oduction factories in Christchurch and
Wellington and heated up like TV dinners in the wards. There is already a preferred
provider being indicated, which is multinati onal company Compass. What is indicated
is that it will have a 15-year  contract, so no one else wi ll get a look-i n. This proposal
will be in place by the end of the year. Compass is proposing to use its product called
Steamplicity, which is pretty common in th e UK. You do not have to go far online to
find out all of the issues there have been a bout food in hospitals in the UK, but they are
currently trialling it at Hillmorton Hospital. I am told that even the potatoes there are
imported from Holland. In a country like New Zealand, it is importing even the
potatoes.
At the same time, this is happening when the Government is proposing to make
major changes to the laws that protect food service workers in hospitals and throughout
the country, and that is with the changes to  Part 6A of the Empl oyment Relations Act,
which I understand will be introduced very  shortly. But it is typical because the
Government always picks on the lowest paid when it comes to changes. It always goes
after the food service workers. It always goe s after the cleaners. It always goes after the
orderlies.
It has done it before. We have been down this path before, and it has failed. In 1993,
when that member Nick Smith was in Government, a National Government brought into
New Zealand a new company called Tempo Services. It came to town promising
hospitals and the Government massive savings on food service production and cleaning.
What we saw was large-scale job losses— massive job losses—and cuts to pay and
hours of work. It even subcontracted its wo rk to another cateri ng operation to avoid
rights. In 1995 it changed its name to Tem po Delaware North Corporation to provide
the expertise and capital to implement a cook -chill catering system, which is similar to
what is being proposed today. After it unsuccess fully tried to increase its contract rate,
the corporation then tried to cut the wo rkers’ wages by 25 percent. It failed. The
workers refused. The corporation left town with its tail between its legs, owing money
up and down the country. Let us not go there again.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The test in the general debate
this afternoon, and for any pa rty in Government, is how a Government deals with the
tough issues that come on the Government’s pl ate. This is a Gove rnment that has had
more than its share of tough issues. What I have witnessed in the House this afternoon is
how fit John Key and his Government are to deal with those tough issues, and how unfit
members opposite are to deal with those issues. What I have witnessed is an Opposition
that is more interested in getting into gr ubby personality pol itics than dealing with the
issues that are relevant. I want to ta lk about the issues at the Government
9240 General Debate 10 Apr 2013
Communications Security Bureau . I want to talk about th e issues of the economy. I
want to respond to the issues that have been raised around the issues of healthcare.

items.speaker: Let us be honest
items.text: the Government Communicat ions Security Bureau  is in trouble. It
has got challenges. It has got challenges that go way past the period that we have been
in Government—way beyond. What we know  is that the bureau was operating
potentially outside the law under the previous Government.
What would a responsible Government do ? A responsible Government would get a
respected public servant to turn that organisation inside out. That is exactly what the
Minister responsible for the GCSB, Prime Minister John Key, has done—exactly what
he has done. What it has shown is that ther e is a question mark about our Government
Communications Security Bureau complying with a law that was written by members
opposite. What it has shown is that duri ng a good period under Helen Clark that
organisation potentially acted unlawfully. We are a Government that is fit to fix it.
What do members opposite want to do? Well, I have to tell you, they have learnt
nothing. They believe that what the public  out there wants to do when we face
challenges is to get down into the gutter and try to besmirch people like our Prime
Minister, and we on this side of the House sa y we will not tolerate it. We have the best
Prime Minister that this count ry has seen in 25 years. He  is a Prime Mi nister who is
prepared to deal with the difficult issues.
What we also saw—and this is the part that is really sad for our country. On issues of
national security, I thought MPs would put their country first—I thought they would put
their country first. What we have seen in speeches from the opposite side of the House
is that when it comes to politics or the na tional interest the Labour  Party and the Green
Party will always choose their political interest over the count ry’s interest. I was
particularly fearful of what I heard from the Green Party. What the Green Party said is
that it wants to scrap the Government Communications Security Bureau—scrap the
Government Communications Security Bur eau. In this time when the threat of
cybercrime is higher than ever, when all of the international thoughtful press is actually
saying that the security threats this century are far more likely in the era of
communications security, we have Opposition pa rties saying that they want to scrap the
organisation. Well, the voters have got a cl ear choice: a National G overnment that will
fix the bureau, or an Opposition that will either play politics with it or get rid of it. I say
that is awfully wrong.
Let us go elsewhere. Let us look at the economy. No Government in a generation has
faced as difficult economic challenges not of its making as this John Key Government.
What this Government has done around th e economy is something of which I am
hugely proud. Let us look at what the IMF has got to sa y about this Government’s
economic record. We have Christine Lagarde,  the Managing Direct or of the respected
IMF, who says if you look at the numbers, whether it is growth, employment, inflation,
debt, or stability, New Zealand looks very promising—in fact, she said “… it’s certainly
a lot better than … [any] other parts of the world.” That is what the IMF is saying about
this Government’s stewardship of the economy. I say again that it shows that this is a
Government that is prepared to front up to the difficult issues not of its making—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has
expired.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I want to tell this House a story, not a fairy
tale, which we have heard from the Govern ment benches, but a true story about the
history of the political life of one Mr John Key, for its benefit. It all started on Waiheke
Island, where he turned up with a $200-plus bottle of Larose  wine to impress his mates
in the National Party so he could get the shoulder-tap to become an MP for National.
So, having influenced them with a $200 bottle of wine, they said: “Oh, we had better
10 Apr 2013 General Debate 9241
have this John Key. He looks like he is a hi gh roller. He is going to bring us a lot of
money.” One year later it is October 2003, and he becomes a member of Parliament. He
returns from New York, having been a mone y trader there for Merrill Lynch. At the
time Don Brash is challenging leader Bill English for the leadership of the National
Party. On the night before th e vote, honest John Key, as they  thought he was, visits Mr
Bill English at his home. He promises Mr English that he will support him in the
morning in the leadership vote—he promises Bill English he will support him. English
and his supporters rejoice.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What do you know?

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Listen to this because you might need to know this history.
Backbenchers, you will need to know this when you are doing a leadership reshuffle.
Anyway, English and his suppor ters rejoice because they are now confident of the
numbers that they have got to retain the leadership. Alas, the morning comes. The vote
is held. To everyone’s shock Don Brash wins by a single vote. The one vote comes
from who? The smiling assassin, John Key. He  double-crosses Bill English. Is it not
incredible! The very same John Key who the night before had promised Bill English his
support did not support him. He turned a nd gave his support to Don Brash, and Don
Brash carried on into the leadership.
The same John Key then carried on to bu ild his political car eer supposedly on
integrity. This is the same John Key who in Opposition railed against corruption,
demanded transparency, and pledged to uphold his Ministers to the very highest of
ethical standards in all their conduct. But le t us not forget this was the same John Key
who forgot to declare his fina ncial interests in Tranz Rail . This is the same John Key
who forgot about an incriminating email about  the Exclusive Brethren. This is the same
John Key who swore black and blue that he di d not know about his blind trust, only to
be video-recorded boasting about his shares in that very same vineyard.
What is more, this is the same John Key who promised not to increase GST, only to
go and do so. This is also the same John Ke y who promised to open the Government’s
banking with Westpac to competition. What di d we get? Simon Power working for the
Westpac bank. That was opening it to compe tition. This is the same John Key who told
everyone he had never met with Steven Joyce’s former company MediaWorks to
discuss a $43.3 million loan, despite the fact that he had. This is the same John Key who
blabbed that Standard and P oor’s would give New Zealan d a credit downgrade if it
elected a new Government, even though Standa rd and Poor’s utte rly rejected that
suggestion made by John Key.
This is the same John Key who apparently cannot remember when the Government
Communications Security Bureau first advi sed him of the spying on Kim Dotcom, and
also could not remember shoul der-tapping his mate Ian Fletch er for the job as Director
of the bureau.
The list goes on and on. Do we see a pattern here? Do we see a pattern? It beggars
belief that we have a Prime Minister who cannot recall intelligence briefings and also
has times when he cannot remember what the tr ue story is. It is tr uly incredible. He is
very economic with the truth—v ery economic with the truth. It  is truly incredible. Not
even Hollywood would come up with a plot as extraordinary as we have seen with this
Dotcom - Government Communications Security  Bureau affair. The Prime Minister is
asking us to believe that either he is the victim of an incredible set of coincidences that
make it appear as though there is something to hide, or he really does have something to
hide. What we want to know is what the true answer is. We—New Zealand First—and
other parties are calling for an independent inquiry into this to get to the bottom of it.
From the facts of this matter, we cannot  trust John Key to do anything. The National
Party certainly cannot trust him. Let us have an inquiry.
9242 General Debate 10 Apr 2013

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: One thing is for sure: that story would
be a great cure for insomnia—there is no doubt about that. I want to speak about some
of the good things that  have happened in my electorate of Rodney. In transport,
investment continues in the de sign and construction of the P ūhoi to Wellsford road of
national significance. This road is extrem ely important to the people of Rodney for
regional economic growth, redu cing congestion, improved sa fety, and reliable journey
times. I would invite any of the members oppos ite to come to Rodney and visit and see
just how important this is to the people of Rodney and Northland.
In health, in Rodney four midwives and 36 nurses have registered to work in hard-to-
staff specialties or communities in the Waitematā District Health Board area through the
Government’s Voluntary Bonding Scheme. Th is is an example of Rodney directly
benefiting from National’s Voluntary Bonding Scheme.
In education, the Government has set a ta rget of 85 percent of 18-year-old school-
leavers attaining National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 2 or
above by 2017. In the final 2011 figures, Rodney had 771 school-leavers sitting NCEA
level 2 or above. With 624 attaining it, that is an 81 percent success rate. To reach 85
percent, our electorate will need an extra 31 students attaining NCEA level 2. Working
together, we will achieve this.
I come to the Ultra-fast Broadband Initia tive. From July 2013 the following Rodney
schools will have ultra-fast broadband: Red Beach School, Stanmore Bay School,
Whangaparaoa School, Whangaparaoa Co llege, KingsWay School, and Mahurangi
College. By the end of 2015, 97.7 percent of schools and 99.9 percent of students will
have access to ultra-fast broadband.
When I was privileged enough to be elected as the representative of the people of
Rodney, I understood clearly th at my life and the life of my family were about to
change. With the responsibility of providi ng leadership and adva ncing and protecting
the interests of my communities also came the acceptance that my life, actions, and
character would be subjected to a high level of public scru tiny and require a high level
of transparency. One of the first tests of th is level of honesty and transparency is the
completion of the Register of Pecuniary a nd Other Specified Interests of Members of
Parliament statement that I was required to make. Every parliamentarian understands
the importance of this document. It is not a document that you take 10 minutes to
complete. It is something that every single one of the MPs who sit in this House makes
sure they have right.
Most of us have a mortgage and financial commitments that  we try to plan for, and
$50,000 is a hugely significant amount of mone y for any Kiwi family working to get
ahead. How on earth did the leader of the La bour Party, the man who wants to become
the Prime Minister, forget an offshore bank account containing at least $50,000, and
probably a lot more than that? The thing that  I find incredible, and I feel brings Mr
Shearer’s decision-making ability and credib ility into serious question, is that the
money that he failed to disclose was that ea rned while he was working in environments
where bribery, kickbacks, corruption, and fraud were prolific, where there is a history of
UN officials—often in very senior roles —having been investig ated, charged, and
convicted for serious fraud, with the ill-gotten gains often being recovered in accounts
around the world, including New York.
I have stated publicly and in this House previously that I rec ognise and respect the
work that Mr Shearer has done around the world in delivering aid—something close to
my own heart. But he has shown a stunning lack of judgment by failing to declare this
account, not 1 year but 4 years in a row. Once you could forgive, twice is harder to
ignore, but three or four times must bri ng into question intent. The Leader of the
Opposition must consider that he has failed to  disclose money that he has put into an
10 Apr 2013 General Debate 9243
offshore account that was likely to have been deposited while he was working in
conditions where there are regul ar accusations of kickbacks a nd bribes. If he wants to
remove doubt, then he must be prepared to front up and explain.
Finally, we have been caught in a global economic storm for the past 5 years. We
have watched bigger economies than ours founde r, breach, and take on water. But we
have had a Prime Minister at our helm who has hunkered down and kept us pointed into
the wind and moving forward, when others are failing and sinking.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: What an outrageous set
of almost accusations from that member over there, Mark Mitchell. Let us talk about the
difference between the mistake that David Shearer made and what has been happening
with John Key. David Shearer made a mistak e. When he realised he had made a
mistake, he stepped up, he we nt forward, and he said: “Guy s, I’ve made a mistake.” He
went down to the press gallery and he told them what the story was. What does John
Key do? When John Key knows he is in trouble, what is his first inclination? His first
inclination is to cover it up, tell half the truth, obfuscate, and stand there and let the truth
drip out bit by tiny bit. It is  like pulling fingernails, trying to get the truth out of John
Key. And that is why New Zealanders are losing confidence in this National-led
Government. That is why New Zealanders are losing confidence in John Key, because
they know they cannot trust him. They cannot  trust him. They cannot trust this John
Key-led Government to be working for them.
New Zealanders cannot trust the Government to protect them from illegal spying.
They cannot trust John Key. When he f ound out, when he was the first Minister
responsible for the GCSB to be told that  the Government Communications Security
Bureau had been carrying out illegal spying on New Zealanders, he did not step in and
say: “New Zealand, this is what is happe ning and I’m going to put  a stop to it.” He
covered it up for months. He held the truth ba ck for months. He refused to tell the truth
until he was put in a position where he had no choice. That is the difference.
New Zealanders cannot trust this Government  to protect their information, to protect
their privacy. It does not matter whether it  is the Earthquake Commission, the ACC,
Work and Income, the Inland Revenue Department and now Novopay’s Talent2, and
even at the Ministry of Justice people’s info rmation is leaking like a sieve, leaking like
this Government, because New Zealanders  cannot trust National to keep their
information private. And what does the Prime Minister say? That he is relaxed about
it—he is relaxed about it. People’s sensitive information is being made available to who
knows whom, and John Key is just relaxed about it. That is because he is not working in
New Zealand’s interests or in the intere sts of New Zealanders. Who does John Key
work for? He works for his mates. That is who John Key works for. That is what the
asset sales are all about—taking assets that all New Zealanders own and putting them
out so that his mates can buy them all up. Th at is who John Key is working for—his
mates and multinational companies.
The latest we have seen of this is this ridiculous proposition from Simon Bridges to
ban protesting by environmental protesters. We live in New Zealand, Simon Bridges,
one of the most open democracies in the worl d, where protest is acceptable. But who is
Simon Bridges working for? He is worki ng for some faceless, foreign multinational
corporation. That is who Simon Bridges and John Key are working for, not for New
Zealanders. It was the same deal with S kycity—not working in the interests of New
Zealanders and not working in the interest s of reducing problem gambling; working for
John Key’s mates at Skycity. And what about The Hobbit ? This Government is not
there to uphold workers’ rights or workplace law and not there to make sure that we are
the shining beacon of industrial relations that we have always been. It is there to work
for Warner Bros, a multinational corporation—John Key’s mates again.
9244 General Debate 10 Apr 2013
Of course, let us not forget the director s at Mighty River Powe r, who received a 73
percent pay increase when the shares in Mighty River Power are being ripped away
from hard-working New Zealanders. And who gets the benefits? It is John Key’s mates,
who are the directors of Mighty River Power.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: They didn’t even ask for it.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: They did not even ask for it. This is just what this
Government does. It is there for its buddies, not for ordinary New Zealanders. But, hey,
we have known this for some time. We ha ve known that John Key’s memory is a bit
shonky. He could not come up with a straight answer if his life depended on it. There
were the Tranz Rail shares, the South Afri can tour, the drinking age, the Dotcom
briefing, calling his buddy Ian Fletcher, and being told that the Government
Communications Security Bureau was actin g illegally. Did he front up? No. Why?
Because New Zealand cannot trust John Key.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: It is an interesting thing to respond
to such a bellowing individual as that one who has just resumed his seat, Iain Lees-
Galloway. I believe he is one of your genuine ou tcasts in this House. He is the kind of
guy who would have never fitted in at a certain private sch ool because he was a lefty.
He certainly does not fit in with his own m ob, because he is a King’s College boy in a
funny old line-up of socialists  and watermelons. And, of course, he was sacked as the
defence spokesperson—he did not get to mini sterial level. So there you have a guy who
just blathers on.
He is similar, of course, to the fifth-lowest polling candidate in the election for the
North Shore, the failed former mayor, A ndrew Williams. There was an individual in
whom no one had any confidence whatsoever. Instead of hearing something sensible,
which, of course, never emerges, what we h eard was an attack on the integrity of the
most popular leader in politics in the last 25 years, as Nick Smith said. I would say that
it is probably about the last 40 years. Bu t this is where you come from when you are
struggling desperately to be the deputy leader : “Pick me! Pick me!”, said Andrew, “I’m
the one!”. There are a few who have prove d themselves totally incapable in New
Zealand First—or “Winston First”, whatever it is called. But he is yet to come in on that
one, because the smart money is on him being the next one to fall over while he is
watering trees.
But let us get back to the reality of what this Government is all about. I am very
proud to be part of a Government that actu ally understands the cr itical importance of
effective resource management to New Zeal and’s economic, environmental, and social
well-being. Unlike the previous speakers from other parties, I would like to concentrate
on some of the matters of substance, rather  than personal attacks. The Minister of
Finance, Bill English, in outlining our Bu siness Growth Agenda, has emphasised the
importance of the Resource Management Act reforms and water management. These are
important to our overall economy. As we know —on this side of the Chamber at least—
job growth will emerge from a strong ec onomy, not from a whole lot of unfounded
rhetoric and rewriting of history, which is what the Opposition specialises in.
As a member of the Local Government and Environment Committee, ably led by our
chair, Nicky Wagner, we have begun h earings on our Resource Management Act
discussion document. On Monday we heard 60  submissions. This is a robust document.
It is one that actually inv ites people to come in and make submissions—ones that we
will consider, because we need to ensure that the overall purpose of the Resource
Management Act reforms remain intact. Fo r example, section 5 is promoting the
sustainable management of natural and physic al resources, and that includes the life-
supporting capacity of air, water, soil, and ecosystems. These are proposals that also
provide that environmental matters of nationa l importance in section 6 of the Resource
10 Apr 2013 General Debate 9245
Management Act are also all being maintain ed. So when it comes to our waterways,
effectively the changes proposed in that s econd phase of the Resource Management Act
go much further than just simply maintaini ng protections, which was about all that the
last incarnation of a failed Labour-Greens G overnment could manage when it had the
chance.
Nick Smith earlier actually questioned the loyalty and the patriotism of the Greens
because of the way that they have a pproached the Government Communications
Security Bureau and a lot of issues. I woul d wonder, really, whether on a daily basis the
Greens betray their own oath of allegiance to th is House, which is to  stay loyal to this
country. I believe that they do. I think that the constant opposition and undermining
does this country no good at all. They do not  serve the environment well and they do
not serve the country th ey live in well, but maybe that is because they have got a co-
leader who does not come from here. Do you think that might have something to do
with it? Who knows?

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Note they haven’t objected.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: They have not objected; no, th ey have gone very quiet. They
tend to do that when facts ar e put in front of them. This John Key - led Government, by
contrast, has prioritise d action in this very important area, and we have introduced via
the Resource Management Act national bottom lines for the quality of our waterways.
That is the very first time in New Zeala nd’s history that water quality has been
prioritised in this way.
In the North Shore, my electorate, wh ere I represent a group of people who are
interested in business, my constituents have come to me with a lot of complaints. They
have said that the Resource Management Ac t processes are very time-consuming, they
are very cumbersome, and they are very cos tly, and those constituents have urged us to
reform them. These reforms are really l ong overdue. The Resource Management Act
system, I have been told by my constituents and by the submitters who have come to
our select committee, is unfortunately diffi cult to understand and use, and the North
Shore businesses believe it is  actively discouraging inve stment and motivation. The
Resource Management Act proposal is that the decision makers must recognise and
provide for the value of public access to and along the coastal marine area, the wetlands,
the lakes, and the rivers. These are the sorts of things that we put out for consultation.
We are very satisfied that the provisions that we have outlined will very adequately and
properly provide for those matters, and we are looking forward to receiving more
feedback through the submissions.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
