items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: My contribution, I hope, will be somewhat different in
tone. I want to reflect on some of the events of the week in the health sector. First of all
I will pick up on the statement released today by the College of Public Health Medicine,
which is the professional body representi ng those doctors who are the experts in
preventing illness in New Zealand. What they had to say today was that the long-term
effects of child poverty will be  too costly for the health and prosperity of all New
Zealanders. They finger child poverty as the No. 1 health problem in this country.
That comes on the heels of yesterday’ s announcement of research from the
University of Canterbury that linked Ne w Zealand’s high rates of childhood asthma,
some of the very highest in the world, with  New Zealand’s cold, damp housing stock.
Again, that is pretty congruent with what the college had to say today.
And then the day before yesterday, we read in the newspaper that the Ministry of
Health had reviewed the Government’s $24 million campaign on rheumatic fever. What
it had to say was that although that camp aign was achieving some good things, it was
failing to tackle the fundamental causes of the rheumatic fever epidemic, and therefore
would fail in its central object ive of stamping out the rheumatic fever epidemic in New
Zealand.
Again, those fundamental causes of the epidem ic that the ministry drew attention to
were our stock of overcrowded and da mp housing, poverty—once again—and access to
medical care for the poorest New Zealanders . So we have had a week—3 days so far
this week—where one wonders what tomorro w will bring. In those 3 days those same
factors again and again are being drawn attention to.
New Zealand has, in addition to one of the highest rates of asthma in the developed
world, one of the very highest rates of rheumatic fever. The Government’s attention was
drawn to this in 2010 by the Public Health Advisory Committee, which found that New
Zealand has a rheumatic fever rate 14 times the OECD average—14 times. That is an
outrage, and it is a scandal.
The problem with the approach the Gove rnment has taken—the reason why it will
fail—is that the Government has not understood something very basic about how health
outcomes actually get formed. The Government has a model that is based on individual
risk factors and individual be haviour such that it cannot unde rstand or deal with the big
social and environmental issues that actually shape health outcomes. So poverty, it does
not understand; overcrowding, it does not understand; racism, it does not understand;
and it does not intervene in those factors as a result.
10 Apr 2013 General Debate 9247
The Public Health Advisory Committee report, which I mentioned, set out a
programme of action to deal with those systematic factors that were driving not only the
rheumatic fever epidemic and not only asthma but all of those other big health problems
that this country faces. So far, the Government has failed to act on virtually every aspect
of that plan, apart from one.
The one element that the Government has so  far contributed posit ively to has been
the Warm Up New Zealand campaign, a progra mme of action that the Green Party has
been pleased to be part of and to work on, in partnership with the Government. Some
200,000 New Zealand homes have been insula ted, and the homes that have been
insulated so far have brought this country  around an estimated $1.3 billion worth of
benefits, and yet it seems that  that programme may be in doubt for the future. What the
Green Party says to the Government is that a warm, well-insulated home for every Kiwi
family is not a “nice-to-have”; it is something that is a health necessity. We look
forward to continuing to work with the Government in the future on that programme.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: Is it not wonderful to get into something
positive for a change—the ongoing saga of our  growing economy—instead of dealing
with issues, to quote the Hon Annette King, straight out of Mad magazine, something
that I think we have spent a fa ir bit of this afternoon dealin g with, frankly? I also heard
Steffan Browning referring to my home to wn of Tangimoana this afternoon. He was
speaking of it as though it was some alien village, and I am sure it is not—I live there.
The past few months have been very te sting for many in rural New Zealand. The
drought, a significant event across the North Island, has had a significant effect on many
parts of our farming community. It will also  have a long-term effect on many of our
rural communities and the economic activity that takes place in those towns. I also want
to very briefly mention at the same time the other thing that I think is a significant drain
on rural New Zealand, and that is the meat in dustry and the lower sheep meat prices we
have been suffering from at this present time. Both of those issues are going to
compound in the near future, and certainly probab ly in the next 2 years in the future, of
our hill country in New Zealand.
I want to talk about a coupl e of the bright lights on th e horizon. Certainly, the dairy
industry in the last few weeks has had a signi ficant lift in price, giving new confidence
and buoyancy to that sector. I am sure that that is going to as sist greatly in the recovery
from the drought. The other issue I want to  mention briefly—and I think it is very
important to us—is the log market. It is a pparent by the large number of logging trucks
lumbering, I guess, down our roads on a daily basi s to our ports that this industry is in a
time of buoyancy that it has not seen for so me time. As more and more wood comes to
the market in the next few years, it will increase the pressure on our roads, further
justifying the Government’s  roads of national significan ce programme and making the
work—particularly in my area from Levin to Wellington, or the Wellington Northern
Corridor, including Transmission Gully, as it  is known—even more relevant to our
futures in the lower North Island. Although Labour  and the Greens appear to totally fail
to understand the value of these roading de velopments to our economy, the people in
my electorate, Rangit īkei, and, oddly enough, the people of  Palmerston North stand to
gain significantly from massive efficien cy and cost savings created by these new
roading systems. For example, we will be able to move an extra truck and trailer-load of
logs from the lower end of my electorate to the port of Wellingt on on a daily basis,
making those trucks almost 30 percent more e fficient. That is a significant productivity
gain for the lower North Island.
I talked of the drought in the North Island ha ving seriously affected the ability of our
farmers, and it has seriously affected the ability of our farmers to bank anything.
Unfortunately, they all fully understand the content of their bank accounts. Certainly,
9248 General Debate 10 Apr 2013
many would love to suffer from  the affliction suffered by the Leader of the Opposition,
that of not needing to remember what they have or do not have in their bank accounts.
I wish to commend the perfor mance of Federated Farmers during the course of this
recent drought, and record the fact that I believe that they have been outstanding in their
efforts to assist farmers. They strive fo r solutions to what is certainly a serious
economic event for our rural towns and, ind eed, our farmers. It also needs to be
recorded here, I think, that our farmers have become much more resilient over the years,
and for the most part have very good contingency plans in place to manage this type of
event. The difference in this in stance is that this drought has affected places such as the
West Coast and the Taumarunui and Taihape area, which is certainly a rare event.
There are some very positive things happening in my region. Over the hill in John
Hayes’ electorate, the Wairarapa, we at last have an oil rig setting up business. I hate to
say that it is in John Hayes’ region, and I ha te to say “Watch out, Taranaki.”, but I can
confidently say that the Hawke’s Bay will be  the next oil boom in  New Zealand. I hope
the Opposition can again get its head around that.
I also want to briefly touch, as Maggie Barry has, on the Resource Management Act
reforms. I have had the privilege, I guess, of hosting or being pa rt of a number of
forums on the Resource Management Act in  recent weeks, and I think we will make
some very positive progress in this area. It will lift the shackles from many of our
growth initiatives and improve our environmental responsibility at the same time. Often,
one finds that when you give people their head, they take  responsibility they did not
take before.
This Government has made some great progress with its po licies to grow our
economy when much of the rest of the world is suffering from the malaise of the global
financial crisis. I want to just very quickly refer to a couple of fi gures that I think are
really interesting. One is the growth of trade with China from 2007 until now. In 2007
that trade was around the $2 billion mark. It is now around the $6.9 billion mark—an
extraordinary gain. At the same time, trad e with the UK has moved from $1.6 billion to
$1.3 billion. I think that speaks for the change in our environment. Thank you.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: What a disappointment it wa s that the Minister of
Energy and Resources himself declined leave for this bill to go back to the Commerce
Committee so that the proper scrutiny could be applied to  Supplementary Order Paper
205, which the Minister decided to produce on Easter Sunday, a mere couple of weeks
after the committee had reported back to this House. The Minister, of course, has then
gone on to say that he has been thinking about  this for a long time and that it was well
flagged. My question to the Mini ster in the chair is, why was it not flagged at all with
the select committee? At no point during the process was the select committee told that
this was being worked on, that this was bei ng proposed, or that th is was needed. Why,
when the Local Government and Environment Committee was considering the
Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Sh elf (Environmental Effects) Bill, where
we had broad-ranging discussi ons about our international ob ligations under the United
Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, was th is never raised as an issue in terms of
being compliant with our international obl igations? Why was the select committee not
given the ability to scrutinise  this particular Supplementary Order Paper? What was the
Minister afraid of, that he needed to hold on to this, keep it secret, until the select
committee had reported back to the House? Well, I think we know the answer to this. It
is an utter dog of a Supplementary Order Pape r. There really is no other description for
it.
We have got this National Government, which presided over the worst economic
record in 51 years and which has no plan for the economy apart from oil and gas
exploration, and mining. That  is it. Regardless of wh at you might think of those
activities, it makes sense to be doing other things as well. This is the problem the
National Government has. It has put all its e ggs in this one basket. If this does not fly—
and so far it has not flown in the way th at National thought it would. We have had
Exxon Mobil pull out, we have had Petrobr as pull out, and we have had Apache
Corporation pull out. This is a high-risk area. The likelihood of finding commercial
returns is very small. It is incredibly risky.  In fact, the Government is negligent in its
duty to the people of this country by putting all its eggs in this one basket. This is all the
Government has in terms of economic developm ent. It is not doing anything else. So if
this does not work, then the Government is kind of stuffed and it knows that.
What the Government is doing is attempting to grease the wheels as much as it can to
reduce standards, to reduce, not even the difficulty, but to make it as easy as possible for
these activities to go ahead, regardless of the outcomes. So the environmental impacts
do not matter. Safety does not matter. Re gardless of the outcomes, this National
Government is ripping the guts out of existin g legislation and is introducing new
legislation to make it as permissive as possible a regulatory environment for these
activities to go ahead. We have only to look in our own country at what happened in
terms of Pike River, overseas in terms of the Gulf of Mexico disaster, and our own
ability to clean up after the Rena disaster. It was not because of a mining activity, but oil
in the water is oil in the water, and no matter where it comes from we need to be able to
deal with that. You have only to look at those risks to real ise that what we need is
robust, effective legislation. What we need is  legislation that prot ects the environment
and ensures as much as we can that where th is activity goes ahead it is done safely and
it is done to the absolute highest standards.
9250 Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill 10 Apr 2013
Instead, what we have in the Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill is
the opposite. The Minister’s Supplementary Order Paper 205, whic h is about stopping
people from protesting against oil and gas e xploration in the excl usive economic zone,
is an absolute outrage of a Supplementary Or der Paper. If it was not, then the Minister
would not have announced it on Easter Sunday and he would have se nt it to the select
committee. His own behaviour shows us that this is not something that he wanted to be
scrutinised on. He has consistent ly refused to front up to medi a, to do interviews on it,
to talk about it—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: He’s on the TV all the tim e. Every time you switch it
on he’s there. What are you talking about?

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Jonathan Coleman is jealous that apparently Simon Bridges is
getting too much TV time. Unfortunately, Mr  Coleman, Mr Bridges is not talking about
the issue of Supplementary Order Paper 205, wh ich is what people wanted to talk to
him about.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Who’s interested in that, for God’s sake?

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Who is interested in that? How about the 10,000 people who
have signed up in support of the Greenpeace legal opinion in 24 hours?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: The sad lefties.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Mr Coleman calls them the sad lefties. People who want to
protect the right to protest are sad lefties. They are probably knuckleheads as well. Well,
that shows the arrogance of this National- led Government. I see the Attorney-General
hovering there, ready to jump to his feet, no doubt in some de fence of Minister Bridges.
But the reality is that when you look at the le gal minds who have said that this is an
outrage, it is clear—[Bell rung] Mr Chairman.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The honourable Moana Mackey.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Thank you—a very good decision, Mr Chair. When you look
at the legal opinion that Gree npeace produced, it is clear that at the very least this
Supplementary Order Paper needs to go back  to the select comm ittee so it can have
proper scrutiny. If this was about safety—the Mi nister says it is about two things. It is
about safety and it is about meeting our international obligations.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Yep.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Well, if that was the case, Mr Coleman, why would we not
extend the Maritime Transport Act and the Crim es Act, which cover this activity in our
territorial waters, into the exclusive economic zone? Then it would cover all vessels and
all dangerous and illegal behaviour, for any reason. Oh, now he is reading something.
He is pretending to read. I am sorry. I will not interrupt you. I will not interrupt you
while you are pretending to read, Mr Coleman.
But the reality is that this applies only to protest vessels, and it applies only to protest
vessels that are protesting ag ainst oil and gas exploration. Yesterday when the Minister
was doorstopped by the media, he said as much. “I don’t know why they’re
complaining that this is a br each of people’s rights, becaus e it is only protesting against
oil and gas exploration that we are stoppi ng. The anti-whaling stuff can go ahead. The
antinuclear stuff can go ahead.” Well, actually th at is the problem. If this is about safety
and if this is about bridging a gap in our  international obligations—apparently the
Minister thinks that we are not compliant  with the convention. Well, actually the
convention talks only about inst allations. It does not talk about vessels at all. The
convention is also very, very strong on the rights of navigati on. So what the Minister is
doing here with his 500-metre zones where these boats cannot go in is actually contrary
to the convention. But in reality the National Government really does not care about the
convention, otherwise it would not have passed the exclusive economic zone legislation.
We know that that is just a smokescreen.
10 Apr 2013 Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill 9251
But here is a very simple question, Mini ster. If this is a bout safety and our
international obligations, why would we not  extend the regime that exists in our
territorial waters in to the exclusive economic zone and cover every vessel and every
incidence of dangerous or reckless behavi our? That absolutely should be addressed.
Why are we targeting only one group of vessels? Silence—there is absolute silence. The
reason we are targeting only one particular gr oup of vessels is that this is all about
sending a very strong message to the oil a nd gas industry that this Government is
prepared to do anything for investment. We have legislation for sale, once again. The
Minister said that, yes, he had been lobbied about this an d he had met with companies
that had complained to him about what had happened around Petrobras on the East
Coast.
I tell you what. No one from the Government ever fronted up on the East Coast to the
public meetings or to the community forums. One was run by the chamber of
commerce—hardly a left-wing or green or ganisation—and no one from Government,
not even our local MP, would turn up to t hose meetings. There ha ve been plenty of
protests onshore. Minister Bridges said  we should go and prot est at Petrobras’
headquarters. Well, they are in Brazil, so it is a little bit difficu lt. There have been
protests. There have been numerous attempts to get the Government to listen, and the
arrogance of this National-led Government ha s meant that not a single Minister or MP
has fronted up to those commun ity forums. So then, yes, pr otesters have taken their
protests to the seas to try to get the Government’s attent ion, and to tell the Government
that they are concerned that the regulatory regime under which these activities are going
to be operating is not sufficient to protect our  marine environment, to protect our local
economies—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Why don’t they just send an email?

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Minister Coleman says they should just send an email. Well,
they did actually. They have been sendi ng hundreds and hundreds of emails, telling
people they are concerned about this, but th e phone is off the hook with this National-
led Government because this is all they have. This is it. All the eggs are in this basket.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: As I was saying before the dinner break, this is bad legislation
made worse by a very bad Supplementary Orde r Paper in the name of the Minister of
Energy and Resources, Simon Br idges. Why Labour objects to  this legislation—we did
welcome the approaches that were made to us by the previous Minister of Energy and
Resources, Phil Heatley, to try to see wh ether we could find some common ground on
this, because we would like to be able to get as much certainty as possible, but we were
unable to, for a number of reasons. The main  ones being that the shared decision-
making power between the Minister of En ergy and Resources and the Minister of
Conservation is, we believe, entirely inappropriate.
Once again, as I was saying before the dinner break, the National Government has no
other plan—other than oil a nd gas exploration, and mining. Th at is it. That is the sum
total of its economic development plan, and if  it does not work, it has nothing else. So
this is not about not liking o il and gas exploration or not liking mining; this is about
saying that we need to be doing other things as well, in case this does not pan out. As I
said, we have had Exxon Mobil Corporation leave, we have had Petrobras leave, and we
have had Apache Corporation leave. This is not an area where we are certain that,
firstly, they are going to find anything or, secondly, that what they find is going to be in
commercial amounts that are able to be explo ited. So a sensible Government, even if it
was as keen on oil and gas and mineral exploration—
9252 Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill 10 Apr 2013

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I was most interested in
that florid contribution by Moana Mackey before  the dinner break in this debate on the
Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill.  I have been very interested also in
comments about the Minister of Energy a nd Resources’ Supplementary Order Paper
205 that have been advanced by some of our  most distinguished and leading citizens
who say that the proposed amendments breach international law and attack our
democratic freedoms. When I heard that I thought, well, we had better have a good look
at that because they are very serious allegations.
I then found out who were th e authors of the statement.  They were Dame Anne
Salmond, who wrote a most interesting book on  Captain Cook, which clearly qualified
her to speak about the high seas, and former Prime Minister Sir Geoffrey Palmer, who
could only be described as a sort of apotheosis of constitutional virtue, whose voice was
particularly quiet when the foreshore and s eabed legislation was being debated in this
House, mainly—I think, probably—because he was acting for the marine farming
institution, and it was very quiet when the dr eadful Stalinist electoral finance legislation
was going through the House. But it is great to hear that he has found his constitutional
voice again and has been opining at great length, in between talking to Sir Bruce
Ferguson, presumably about Government Comm unications Security Bureau matters, on
Lambton Quay this afternoon.
I took a good look at the legislation a nd was immediately drawn back to Sir
Geoffrey’s lectures in 1975, when he taught me Legal System, because Sir Geoffrey, the
great teacher that he was, said how impor tant it was to focus on the wording of the
legislation. I can recall a la wyer appearing in the Court of Appeal many years ago,
telling the Court of Appeal that there were 12 possible interpretations of a section of an
Act. After about 2½ hours of driving Their H onours nuts, the Presiden t of the Court of
Appeal, then Sir Robin Cooke, said: “Well, there’s the 13 th.” The fellow said: “Well,
what is that, Sir?”. He said: “The plain meaning.” I really th ink that this is a situation
where if one gets away from the hyperbole, if one gets away from  the purple prose and
the waffle and the politically inspired crit icism of the Supplementary Order Paper and
focuses rather on the wording of the legislation, one sees that the answer is tolerably
clear.
I come to new section 101B in new cl ause 46A and note that it has nothing
whatsoever to do with protest. People are fully entitled to exercise their democratic right
to protest. What that clause, which my fr iend the Minister of Energy and Resources is
seeking to introduce here, deals with is th e commission of an offence if damage is
caused under subclause (a), “damage to, or interference with, any equipment ...” under
subclause (b), or “interference with any operations or activities ...” under subclause (c).
So the proposed amendments, which have ex cited the great and the good of the area
inside the beltway—as I say, these apotheoses of constitutional virtue, Sir Geoffrey and
Dame Anne, and other members of the great and good—relate to damage or
interference, not protest. There is no r eason at all why people cannot exercise their
democratic right to protest, but it has to be protest that does  not result in damage to or
interference with—for example,  under subclause (a)—the stru cture or the ship. So it is
quite a straightforward matter—

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: How embarrassing—this is the Attorney-General.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: —and I hear the creatures on the other side
yelling out: “How embarrassing! ”, but I think that Sir Geof frey always said, when he
was teaching me law, to “Focus on the words—focus on the plain meaning.” He did not

10 Apr 2013 Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill 9253
members on the other side of the Chamber. Get away from the purple prose; get away

speeches on the Government Communications Secu rity Bureau. It is all so very simple.

That is why I believe that Sir Geoffrey  and Dame Anne, great people though they

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. If the

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: I do not wish to dwell on this too much in the
short time I have, but I would like to note that as the previous speaker, Hon Chris
Finlayson, has said, words are incredibly im portant and the words on the page are very
important. But delivering sarcasm and drip ping bile and venom ag ainst people who are
not in this Chamber to defend themselves is not what one woul d call parliamentary
behaviour. And I think that that  kind of behaviour against people of great standing—let
us just remember that just recently Dame  Anne Salmond was made New Zealander of
the Year. I did not hear the Attorney-General object to that, and I think it was a very
appropriate award to give her. To come into  this Chamber and use that style of venom,
to which we are accustomed from that me mber, is beneath him, and that patronising
attitude that he takes does not advance the words on the page, to which I come.
I come to the words on the page because the words on the page are inadequate. Let
me speak about this. I want to talk about Supplementary Order Paper 205 in the name of
the Minister of Energy and Resources, and I want to draw attention to a possible
interpretation of Supplementary Orde r Paper 205 that I do  not believe the
Supplementary Order Paper intends or covers  adequately. It comes to the words on the
page, Mr Finlayson. The words on the page th at I am reading, which is printed in the
Bills Digest, say: “the area of the non-inte rference zone to which the activity relates”—
and we are talking about the banning of prot est activity within th is non-interference
zone of structures or ships to which the activity relates; in other words, those that are
working at oil exploration and such activiti es—“(which may be up to 500 metres from
any point on the outer edge of the structure or ship to which the activity relates or, if
there is any equipment attached  to the structure or ship, 500 metres from any point on
the outer edge of the equipment);”.
Given that the National Party is so well-endowed with lawyers, I wonder whether the
Minister could address the issue of this  non-interference area of 500 metres. If, for
example, Greenpeace, in the course of its lawful activity, protesting against oil or
mineral exploration in the deep sea, were to pull up within 500 metres of a ship that was
engaging in that activity, and that ship itself decided to breach the 500-metre limit and
move towards Greenpeace in a threatening ma nner, as we have seen Japanese whaling
9254 Crown Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill 10 Apr 2013
ships do in the face of protests on the high seas, then where is the Minister’s law and
words on the page? Who is breaching the 500-metre limit in that instance?
If they try to provoke democratic and legitim ate protesters into activities that they
will not resile from—in other words, they have done what the law says and pulled up
within 500 metres of a ship that is carrying out this activity—and that ship itself then
broaches the 500-metre limit, who is at fa ult? Who gets the $100,000 fine? Where does
that responsibility lie and w hy has the Minister not got th e words on the page right? He
has got the “archbishop of words on the page” sitting on his ri ght hand, and, really,
quite frankly, I would think—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Cardinal.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: Cardinal-something—cardinal-something. I might come
to that in a later speech on another subject , perhaps—cardinal-something. However, on
this matter, the man who sets himself up as the one with the greatest knowledge of the
words on the page should surely have couns elled his junior colleague and said: “I’m
sorry. You haven’t got the words on the page  quite right.” But in addition to that
carelessness, that sloppiness of drafting, wh at we see from this—because the words on
the page are not accurate, are not sufficient—is the actual design of this Supplementary
Order Paper 205.
I would have supported Gareth Hughes’ pr ocedural motion earlier this evening,
which was not allowed by the Committee, to have this Supplementary Order Paper
referred back to the Commerce Committee so  that people could tease it out and see
whether or not it was appropria te. But this Minister clearly did not want public scrutiny
of this, because, as Paul Buchanan said of the Prime Minister just  last week when he
was talking about the Prime Minister a nd his poor oversight of the Government

items.speaker: Communications Security Bureau

items.text: Order! Members can use examples, but I just
